title: Getting the Derivative You Need Without Building the Whole Table
key_insight: With a giant switchboard, follow only the knob direction or bulb concern you need instead of writing down every hidden wire.
body:
## The Giant Switchboard

Imagine a million knobs connected to a million lightbulbs. Writing how every knob affects every bulb would make a gigantic pile of notes; people call that full pile a Jacobian.

Usually you need less. Nudge a chosen group of knobs and watch all bulbs: that shortcut is a Jacobian-vector product. Choose one bulb and trace its wires backward: that is a vector-Jacobian product.

Forward-gradient research tests a few knob directions instead of tracing every wire backward. It can save stored work, but each test gives a noisier clue, so many clues may be needed.
common_mistakes: Writing the whole knob-to-bulb table when the task asks about only one chosen direction.
Mixing up the two shortcuts — one pushes a knob movement forward, while the other traces a bulb concern backward.
Assuming the forward shortcut is always faster — it depends on how many knob directions and bulb concerns matter.
Treating one randomly chosen direction as the complete answer — it is a noisy clue that usually needs companions.
mini_exercise: Draw three knobs connected to two bulbs. Pick one combined knob movement and describe how you would find both bulb changes without listing every possible movement.
real_world_usage: Differentiation libraries offer forward and backward shortcuts for scientific models, sensitivity checks, and training. These shortcuts answer a chosen direction question without storing the enormous full connection table.
explain_back_prompt: Using the switchboard, explain the full connection table, the push-forward shortcut, the trace-backward shortcut, and why random forward tests can be noisy.
